reason: The biblical narrative in this passage (2 Samuel 13-19) does not support the dichotomy that Yahweh cares exclusively for Hebrew leaders while lacking empathy for the people. The text shows: (1) Divine judgment affects leaders and common people alike—Amnon is killed for his crime against Tamar, David and his household suffer consequences for their transgressions, and Absalom is struck down despite being a leader's son; (2) In the rebellion narrative, 20,000 common soldiers die in battle with no indication of preferential divine concern for either leaders or soldiers; (3) David himself demonstrates deep empathy for his people throughout, suggesting leadership values that reflect divine concern for all. The text presents a complex narrative of consequences and judgment that operates across all social strata, not one showing divine partiality toward leaders at the expense of the people.
